oneSentence: Compute is the processing capacity used to train and run AI systems, with different needs before deployment and during everyday use.
plainExplanation:
Compute means the processing resources needed to make an AI system do work. In practice, that usually means chips, memory and time, plus the electricity and money needed to use them. More compute can let a system handle larger models or more requests, but it does not guarantee better results.

Two related terms are often mixed together. Training compute is the compute used while building a model from examples. This stage can take days or months and usually happens only sometimes. Inference compute is the compute used after deployment, when the model produces an output for a real prompt, image or other input. This stage happens every time someone uses the system.

What goes in depends on the stage. During training, the inputs include training data, model settings and many repeated calculations that adjust the model. During inference, the inputs include a user request and the stored model. What happens is a large number of mathematical operations on specialised hardware. What comes out is either an updated model during training or a prediction, classification or generated response during inference.

Compute is related to, but different from, the hardware itself. A GPU or CPU is a type of processor; compute is the amount of processing work available or consumed on that hardware. It is also different from cloud computing, which is one way to rent and manage those resources, and from cost per token, which is one pricing measure for inference use.

For non-specialists, the key point is simple: compute affects cost, speed, scale and who can access advanced AI. It also has environmental implications because heavy compute use can require significant energy and cooling.

everydayAnalogy.title: Finding and using a book system in a large library
everydayAnalogy.story: A city library wants a faster way to help visitors find books. First, a team spends weeks walking through shelves, checking labels, correcting catalogue records and building a better index for the whole library. Later, when a visitor asks for a book on drought planning in the Sahel, a librarian uses that finished index to answer in seconds. Building the index took a lot of staff time and effort once; using it for each visitor takes much less effort, but it happens again and again all day. If the library gets many visitors at once, it needs more desks or staff on duty to keep responses fast.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library index is built by people using explicit rules, while AI training usually adjusts many numerical parameters through repeated calculations. Also, a librarian can deliberately judge context in ways a model may not. The analogy helps show the difference between building and using a system, but it does not explain the mathematics or the limits of model output quality.

visual.title: Training compute and inference compute
visual.learningObjective: Show the difference between compute used to build a model and compute used each time the model is used, and explain how both affect cost and speed.
visual.description: A two-column comparison. Left column shows training: data enters, many repeated processing rounds happen, and an updated model comes out. Right column shows inference: a user input enters the trained model, one response comes out, and this repeats for every request. Read top to bottom in each column, then compare the cost and timing labels at the bottom.

steps.label: Training inputs
steps.explanation: Examples, model settings and processing resources are prepared for a training run.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column top: icons for data files, model settings sliders and compute chips feeding into a box labelled 'training run'.

steps.label: Repeated training work
steps.explanation: The system performs many rounds of calculation to adjust the model. This often uses large amounts of compute over a limited period.
steps.visualInstruction: Inside the left column box, show looping arrows around small numbered passes, with labels 'many repetitions', 'high compute', 'hours to months'.

steps.label: Trained model output
steps.explanation: The result of training is an updated model that can later be deployed.
steps.visualInstruction: Left column bottom: arrow to a sealed model box labelled 'trained model'.

steps.label: Inference inputs
steps.explanation: After deployment, a real user request is sent to the trained model.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column top: prompt bubble and trained model box entering a box labelled 'inference'.

steps.label: One response per request
steps.explanation: Inference uses compute every time the system produces an answer, image label or prediction. Small per request costs can add up at scale.
steps.visualInstruction: Right column middle and bottom: one arrow to one output bubble, then duplicate request-output pairs fading behind it to show repetition across many users.

steps.label: Decision view
steps.explanation: Training compute is usually a big, occasional investment. Inference compute is an ongoing operational demand that affects speed, cost and scalability.
steps.visualInstruction: Bottom strip spanning both columns with three labelled markers: 'build cost', 'run cost', 'user speed'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each column to highlight its inputs, processing pattern and output; a toggle switches the bottom strip between 'single request' and 'many requests'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares two uses of compute. On the left, training starts with data, model settings and processing resources. These enter a training run that repeats many calculations, shown as loops, and produces a trained model. Labels emphasise high compute use over a limited period. On the right, inference starts with a user request plus the trained model. These enter one inference step and produce one output. The pattern repeats for every new request. A final summary line says training compute is mainly a build-stage cost, while inference compute is a continuing run-stage cost that affects speed and scale.

The left column shows training inputs, repeated passes and a trained model. The right column shows a request, the trained model and one output, plus a row of repeated request-output pairs to indicate ongoing use.

workedExample.scenario: A small organisation tests a translation assistant for public, non-sensitive documents in three languages.
workedExample.input: Model A takes 200 GPU-hours to fine-tune on approved material. After deployment, each user request uses about 2 seconds of GPU time. The pilot expects 15,000 requests per month.
process: The team spends 200 GPU-hours once to adapt the model during training.
The finished model is deployed to a hosted service for staff use.
Each incoming request uses about 2 seconds of inference compute to generate a reply.
At 15,000 monthly requests, total inference time is about 30,000 seconds, or roughly 8.3 GPU-hours for that month.
If demand grows to 300,000 requests, inference compute rises to about 166.7 GPU-hours, even though the training cost stays the same unless the model is retrained.
workedExample.result: The pilot's main compute cost at first is training, but at larger scale the ongoing inference cost becomes the bigger operational issue.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A humanitarian coordination team wants an AI tool to draft first-pass summaries of already approved, non-sensitive situation updates from multiple field offices.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Leaders need to distinguish the one-off compute needed to adapt or evaluate the tool from the ongoing compute needed each time staff generate a summary. That affects budget, hosting choices, response speed and whether the service can handle surges during emergencies.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place confidential, personal, protection-sensitive or security-sensitive information into an unapproved public AI service. Use approved systems, apply human review, and check data governance and hosting arrangements before deployment.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists hear claims about powerful models, but those claims often hide a practical question: how much processing work is required, when, and at what cost. Compute affects whether an AI project is affordable, how quickly it responds, how many people can use it at once, and whether an organisation depends on scarce infrastructure or external providers. It also matters for procurement, environmental impact, continuity planning and equity, because systems that require very large amounts of compute may be harder for smaller organisations or lower-resource regions to access. Understanding the difference between training compute and inference compute helps leaders ask better questions before approving or scaling a system.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More compute always means a better AI system.
commonMisconceptions.correction: More compute can support larger training runs or faster service, but quality also depends on data quality, model design, evaluation and the task itself. A poorly designed system can consume large compute and still perform badly or unsafely.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Compute just means having a powerful chip.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A chip is hardware. Compute refers to the processing capacity available or used on that hardware over time, together with related resources such as memory, electricity and system configuration. The same hardware can deliver very different practical compute depending on setup and workload.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once a model is trained, compute is no longer a major issue.
commonMisconceptions.correction: After training, inference compute continues every time the model is used. For popular services, the ongoing compute for serving users can become a major operational cost and can limit response speed during peak demand.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Compute is the amount of machine processing needed to build an AI system and to run it afterwards. Training compute is the big effort to create or adapt the model; inference compute is the smaller but repeated effort each time someone uses it.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Compute refers to the processing resources consumed to execute numerical operations, usually on accelerators or general processors, over time. In training, compute is used for repeated forward and backward passes that update model parameters using training data. In inference, compute is used for forward passes through a fixed model to produce outputs for new inputs. People sometimes measure compute indirectly through processor time, floating-point operations, throughput or service capacity, but the exact metric depends on context and is not fully standardised across systems. Compute is related to, but distinct from, hardware type, cloud deployment, latency, cost and energy use.

keyTakeaway: Ask two separate questions: how much compute is needed to build the model, and how much is needed every time people use it.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best distinguishes training compute from inference compute?
options: Training compute builds or updates a model from examples; inference compute runs the finished model on new inputs.
Training compute happens in the cloud; inference compute happens only on local devices.
Training compute is about storing data; inference compute is about cleaning data.
Training compute uses CPUs; inference compute uses GPUs.
quickCheck.explanation: The main difference is the stage and purpose. Training compute is used while creating or adapting the model. Inference compute is used after deployment to generate outputs for actual requests. Either stage can use different hardware or locations depending on the system.
